Empirical Research Plan  
“Intergenerational Transmission of Human Capital: Evidence from the Norwegian Compulsory‐Schooling Reform”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: 2-stage least squares (2SLS) IV design embedded in a difference-in-differences (DID) / cohort-event‐study framework.

Why appropriate  
• Endogeneity problem: parents who choose more schooling differ systematically from those who do not.  
• Norway’s compulsory-schooling reform provides plausibly exogenous variation in parents’ years of schooling that is orthogonal to unobserved family traits yet powerful enough to shift education.  
• Treating parental birth cohort × reform exposure as an instrument allows us to retrieve the causal effect of parental education on the child’s educational attainment.  
• A DID/event-study across narrowly spaced birth cohorts allows flexible control for cohort trends and separate testing of identifying assumptions (parallel trends, no pre-trends).

Short description  
Stage 1: ParentEduᵢ = α₀ + π ReformExposure_parent + f(parent birth-year) + X + ε  
Stage 2: ChildEduᵢ = β ŴParentEduᵢ + f(parent birth-year) + X + u  

where ŴParentEduᵢ is the predicted schooling from Stage 1.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• ReformExposure_parent = 1 if the parent entered compulsory school in or after the first academic year in which the new 9-year minimum applied in her municipality; 0 otherwise.  
(If reform was national and simultaneous, the cutoff is common; if staggered, exposure is municipality-by-cohort.)

Control group  
• Parents born in cohorts just before the reform who faced the old 7-year requirement.

Treatment timing / event date  
• National law was passed in 1969; full rollout completed by 1974. Define the cutoff birth cohort as those who TURNED age 7 (school-starting age) in 1969 + rolloutlag_muni.  
Example (national, sharp): birth cohort 1958+ (turned 7 in 1965) unaffected; 1959–1962 partly treated; 1963+ fully treated. We will use the first fully treated cohort as treated.

If rollout varies by municipality, we use municipality-specific implementation year.

Running variable (if we also estimate an RDD robustness check)  
• Parent year-of-birth centered at the first treated cohort; cutoff = 0.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: the reform raised parents’ completed years of schooling.  
– Plausible; Norway saw an average +0.7 to +1.1 years for affected cohorts in historical stats.

A2. Exclusion Restriction: the reform affects children only through parental schooling, not through other channels once we condition on cohort and municipality fixed effects.  
– Plausible because parents finished schooling decades before their children’s outcomes. The law did not alter labor-market conditions differently across adjacent cohorts aside from the schooling itself.

A3. No differential pre-trends (DID): in absence of the reform, child outcomes would have trended smoothly across adjacent parental cohorts.  
– Testable using event-study graphs of placebo leads.

A4. Stable composition / no selective fertility: parental birth-cohort composition did not change discontinuously at the cutoff.  
– Check by plotting parental characteristics versus cohort.

A5. SUTVA / no spillovers across families that violate exclusion.  
– Reasonable; any spillovers (e.g., peer effects across cohorts) likely small and smooth.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats & Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Reform changed other parental outcomes (income, occupation) that themselves affect children.  
Mitigation:  
• Show that conditional on schooling, ReformExposure has no residual effect on income/occupation (over-identification test).  
• Control flexibly for parental earnings in a “bad-control” sensitivity and show β stable.

Threat 2: Cohort or macro shocks coincide with reform.  
Mitigation:  
• Include quadratic parent birth-year trends and municipality × linear cohort trends.  
• Event-study of child outcomes vs. parental birth-year to verify no pre-trend.

Threat 3: Differential migration or fertility around the cutoff.  
Mitigation:  
• Check discontinuity in number of births, parental nationality, and residential municipality at cutoff.  
• Re-estimate on subsamples with stable residence histories; weight by inverse propensity of remaining in Norway.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # IV regressions
library(ggplot2)

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
#----------------------------------------------------------
# Assume the file 'norway_intergen.csv' in working dir
dt <- fread("norway_intergen.csv")

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#----------------------------------------------------------
# a) Parent exposure indicator
dt[, treat_parent := as.integer(parent_birthyear >= reform_cutoff_year_muni)]

# b) Outcome and endogenous regressor
dt[, child_schooling  := child_years_schooling]     # observed at age 30
dt[, parent_schooling := parent_years_schooling]

# c) Controls
dt[, birth_cohort_parent := parent_birthyear]
dt[, birth_cohort_child  := child_birthyear]        # might be used for FE
dt[, muni                := municipality_code]
dt[, X_controls := .(parent_gender, parent_immigrant,
                     child_gender, sibsize, log_family_income)]

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV specification
#----------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- child_schooling ~ 1 + 
              parent_gender + parent_immigrant + 
              child_gender + sibsize + log_family_income | 
              ( . ~ treat_parent )

# Two-way fixed effects: parent cohort and municipality
res_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt,
                fixef = ~ factor(birth_cohort_parent) + factor(muni),
                cluster = ~ birth_cohort_parent)  # cluster at cohort level

etable(res_iv, se = "cluster")

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness check: Event-study graph
#----------------------------------------------------------
# a) Create cohort distance
dt[, cohort_dist := parent_birthyear - reform_cutoff_year_national]

# b) Dummies for each distance -10 … +10
for(k in -10:10) dt[, paste0("coh",k) := as.integer(cohort_dist==k)]

# b) OLS of child_schooling on cohort dummies (excluding -1 as base)
coh_vars <- paste0("coh", setdiff(-10:10, -1))
fml <- as.formula(paste("child_schooling ~", paste(coh_vars, collapse="+"),
                        "+", "parent_gender + parent_immigrant + child_gender + sibsize",
                        "| factor(muni)"))
es_res <- feols(fml, data = dt, cluster=~birth_cohort_parent)

# c) Plot coefficients
es_plot <- data.table(k = setdiff(-10:10, -1),
                      coef = coef(es_res)[coh_vars],
                      se   = se(es_res)[coh_vars])
ggplot(es_plot, aes(k, coef)) +
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=coef-1.96*se, ymax=coef+1.96*se)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  labs(x="Parent birth-cohort distance from cutoff", y="Coef on cohort dummy",
       title="Event-study / pre-trend test")

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Placebo cutoff robustness
#----------------------------------------------------------
for(pl_cut in seq(-8, +8, by=2)){
  dt[, placebo := as.integer(parent_birthyear >= (reform_cutoff_year_national + pl_cut))]
  res_placebo <- feols(child_schooling ~ 1 | . ~ placebo,
                       data=dt, fixef=~factor(birth_cohort_parent)+factor(muni),
                       cluster=~birth_cohort_parent)
  print(c(pl_cut, coef(res_placebo)['parent_schooling']))
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Becker–Tomes, 1979) predicts a positive intergenerational elasticity of human capital. Prior Nordic evidence suggests an IV‐estimated effect of roughly 0.1–0.2 years of child schooling per additional year of parent schooling. I therefore expect:  
β ≈ 0.15 (95 % CI say 0.08–0.22).  
Magnitude likely smaller than OLS, consistent with attenuation toward causal effect.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable ………………………………… 0.8 (~1)  
C3: No manipulation / smooth cohort composition …………… 1  
C4: No other policy confounds around cutoff …………………… 0.8  
C5: SUTVA & no spillovers violating exclusion ………………… 0.8  
Overall (average) ……………………………………………………… 0.88  

(Items scored 1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable; we assign 0.8 where mostly but not perfectly satisfied.)

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
